article.plain_text:
Research supported in part by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) provides new insights into cell processes that happen in people with rheumatoid arthritis before symptoms begin. Learning more about the mechanisms driving the progression of clinical rheumatoid arthritis could help researchers find potential drug targets for preventing disease. The study findings were published in Nature Aging.
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease marked by joint and systemic inflammation. Although treatments can reduce inflammation and slow joint damage, identifying and preventing RA before arthritis develops remains a challenge. One early warning sign is the presence of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs), which recognize the body’s own proteins after a chemical change called citrullination. These antibodies can appear years before arthritis begins, but not everyone with ACPAs develops RA. To better understand why some people develop the disease while others do not, the researchers in this study compared blood samples collected before and after arthritis developed in ACPA-positive individuals with samples from ACPA-positive people who remained arthritis-free and healthy volunteers without ACPAs.
The researchers found that before arthritis developed, people who later developed RA had a higher proportion of a specific type of immune cell called activated naïve B cells. These cells acted like inflammatory and senescent (aged) cells and had receptors that could recognize several different molecules in the body, including proteins, suggesting that they might contribute to harmful immune responses. The researchers confirmed these main findings in additional groups of people at risk for RA and identified similar cells in joint tissue from people with the disease. In lab experiments, these B cells presented citrullinated proteins to T cells, activating another part of the immune system. Repeated exposure to these modified proteins caused normal naïve B cells from people with RA to move into this activated state.
In short, the study suggests that activated naive B cells may contribute to the immune changes that occur before arthritis develops in ACPA-positive individuals. Further research could determine whether measuring these cells helps identify who is most likely to develop RA and whether targeting them could prevent or delay the disease.
Reference: Wu X, et al. Senescent-like activated naïve B cells contribute to the progression to clinical rheumatoid arthritis. Nature Aging. 2026. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-026-01236-6
